lesson.title: Sampling on the Right: The Right Riemann Sum
lesson.summary: A right Riemann sum evaluates the function at the right edge of each subinterval, the mirror image of the left sum, overestimating area under an increasing function and underestimating it under a decreasing one.
lesson.body:
A right Riemann sum makes the opposite choice from the left sum: it uses the right endpoint of every subinterval as the sample point. For a partition x0, x1, all the way to xn, the right sum uses x1, x2, up through xn as the heights, never x0, since that is not the right edge of any subinterval.

The bias flips accordingly. If f is increasing, the right endpoint of each subinterval sits at the high point of that subinterval, so the sum overestimates the exact area. If f is decreasing, the right endpoint sits at the low point, so the sum underestimates. This is the mirror image of the left sum's behavior, and for a monotonic function on a fixed partition, the left and right sums always straddle the true area from opposite sides, one above and one below.

Use the same f(x) = x² on the interval from 0 to 2 with n = 4 and Δx = 0.5. The right endpoints are x1 = 0.5, x2 = 1.0, x3 = 1.5, x4 = 2.0, with function values f(0.5) = 0.25, f(1.0) = 1.0, f(1.5) = 2.25, f(2.0) = 4.0. The right Riemann sum is Δx times [0.25+1.0+2.25+4.0] = 0.5 times 7.5 = 3.75.

Compare that to the exact value, 8/3, about 2.6667. The right sum of 3.75 overshoots it, exactly as predicted since x² is increasing on this interval. Notice that the left sum from the previous chapter, 1.75, and this right sum, 3.75, bracket the true value of about 2.6667 from below and above, and their spread, 3.75 minus 1.75 equals 2.0, is a rough measure of how much uncertainty four rectangles leaves you with. That spread would shrink with more, narrower subintervals.

Right sums build on the same general Riemann sum framework as left sums, differing only in which edge of each subinterval supplies the sample point. Once you know whether a function is increasing or decreasing, you know immediately whether the right sum will land above or below the exact area, without computing anything.
